brief.head: Vulgar familiarity
brief.text: A finance man may find banking regulation easy and monetary policy mysterious, Ajay Shah said. Familiarity says nothing about difficulty; shared metrics protect against it. {101-C06}

brief.head: Float first
brief.text: Monetary policy is easy only when properly structured, Ajay Shah said: an inflation target, a well-composed committee, a floating exchange rate and an open capital account. {#float}

brief.head: No mythological beast
brief.text: It all starts at public choice theory, Ajay Shah said: “The government is not a mythological creature of infinite capability. The government is a deeply flawed creature.” {101-C01}

brief.head: Measure to think
brief.text: Even rough measurement helps, Amit Varma said: “Not everything is precisely measurable, but the more you attempt to measure something, the more clarity you gain in thinking about it.” {#measure}

brief.head: The CM’s calendar
brief.text: The attention of thinkers, researchers and leaders is the most important resource, Ajay Shah said: what a chief minister does from morning to evening decides what gets done. {#cm}

thought.text: Little else is required, but what is required is very, very hard.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, after running Adam Smith’s three essentials through the four tests

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on what the state can do
lead.head: Four tests before the state acts
body: Amit Varma opened the episode in the dark. “I don’t know if you can see us,” he said, and turned the gloom into a parable about the state: intervention was meant to light the way, “but instead it burnt everything to the ground and there is no power anymore.” {101-J01}
He was, he admitted, being a little over-dramatic. The episode, part of the hosts’ series on the state, asked a sober question. When someone demands that the government act, can it actually succeed?
Ajay Shah’s answer is that this question must come first. Implementation constraints, he said, belong on the table right at the start of any policy discussion. {101-C02}

Mainstream Indian debate, he said, “blithely runs forward” from values to action. Judge first what is easy and what is hard, and scarce money and management effort can be rationed: some lovely objectives let go, the winnable ones taken on.
## The toolkit
The toolkit grew out of work by Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock, which Shah and Vijay Kelkar extended. It asks four questions of any proposed intervention.
How many transactions does it involve? How much discretion do the frontline workers have? How high are the stakes? How opaque is the work?

The higher each one scores, the harder the job. Five hundred research grants a year are easy to manage; polio drops for 500 million people are not. A policeman who can jail you holds high stakes; a vaccinator holds none.
Once learnt, Shah said, the toolkit fits in your head, ready for any hostel-room debate on inflation targeting. {101-C03}
Varma noticed that all four tests probe the same gap, between what the state wants and what its employees want.
## Scoring the state

Shah’s chief demonstration is central banking. Monetary policy, properly structured around an inflation target, is easy: a committee of five makes six decisions a year, in public. Financial regulation is hard, and always will be.
Then the hosts built a table on the fly. Elementary schools scored two out of four. A vaccination drive was easy. The judiciary scored three and a half.
Taxation, with high transactions, high discretion, stakes of thousands of crores and complete opacity, was “four on four”. {101-C04}

A hard row is not the end, Shah argued. Monetary policy was once opaque and ruled by a powerful governor; an inflation target, a committee and full transparency hacked it into an easy problem. Good IT systems can do the same by stripping discretion from clerks.
## Smith’s short list
The deepest implication came with Adam Smith, who said little else is needed for a state’s opulence but peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice.

Run those through the four tests, Shah said, and all three are brutally hard. The minimal state, it turns out, is not an easy state, which is why he would refuse every distraction from that core. {101-C07}
Varma added a caution. The metrics measure how hard a job is, not how much it matters, and Smith’s three must be done however hard they are.
The danger, he said, is the drunk who searches for his key under the lamppost, not because he dropped it there but because that is where the light is.
Too many, he worried, settle for “easy problems that are inconsequential and don’t really move the needle”.

second.label: Central banking
second.head: Easy money, hard banks
second.deck: Why Ajay Shah calls monetary policy trivial and financial regulation four on four
body: We tend to see central banking as one blur, Ajay Shah said. The day he saw it as two jobs, one easy and one hard, was one of the happy days of his life. {101-R05}

A modern monetary policy committee should have five members: the RBI governor and four independent private economists. They meet six times a year to hit a 4 per cent inflation target, and each writes down why they voted. {101-S02} “Six transactions a year. That’s it,” Shah said. “For the rest in the year you’re sleeping.”

Financial regulation is the opposite: a thousand firms, some 2,000 touch points a year, judgment calls on whether a loan is an NPA, billions of dollars at stake and supervision in secrecy. {#touchpoints}

quote.text: So for all the hype and mystique around monetary policy, actually it’s a trivial, easy problem.

third.head: No one was saved
body: The state’s real work, Ajay Shah said, is peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice. But these things are hard, so everybody takes some exit ramp or other.
He counts two ramps. The first is welfareism: humanitarian projects that bring the satisfaction of having fed some children lunch, without solving the hard problems. {#ramps}

The second is unique to engineers: build an IT system. Riffing on P. Sainath’s book *Everybody Loves a Good Drought*, Shah and Vijay Kelkar titled a section of *In Service of the Republic* “Everybody Loves a Good IT System”. {101-J11}

“Some software vendor builds an app, some software vendor builds a website, you celebrate, you’ll inaugurate it, nothing will get done,” Shah said. {101-C10} His verdict came from the Beatles’ *Eleanor Rigby*: “No one was saved.” {101-J09}
third.caption: the exit ramps from hard work

p2.title: Easy or hard?
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s four tests of feasibility, argued over with Amit Varma, chapter by chapter

sections.label: The question
sections.head: First ask: can it be done?
sections.caption: asking whether it can be done
body: Amit Varma framed the question. Whether the state should intervene, he said, depends not only on whether the intervention is justified, but on whether it is possible: whether it will work, and how hard or easy it is.
Ajay Shah went further. Implementation constraints, he argued, should come up front in every discussion of public policy. {101-C02}

The hosts’ scepticism has deep roots, and Shah restated four of them. The world is too complex, so the true facts about a society are unknowable to planners. {#unknowable} The incentives of the state’s personnel clash with its objectives. Special interest groups kick the government around. And even well-meant projects are badly implemented.
Hence, he said, the “environment of diffidence” the hosts bring whenever someone says the government will do one new thing.
## A judgment in a flash

Shah’s test case was military. Landings in Burma and in China are both very hard, but anyone can see at once that the first is possible and the second practically impossible. The aim is to make such calls routine for policy. {101-S01}
Mainstream Indian policy, he said, rarely asks the question at all. Yet judging what is easy and what is hard is what lets a government ration its money and management effort.
~ Some lovely objectives, he said, should simply be let go: “We won’t be able to win this one.”

quote.text: We should always bring implementation constraints on the table. Like right up front, start thinking, can we do it?

sections.label: The four tests
sections.head: What makes a job hard
sections.caption: the four tests of difficulty
body: Faced with any problem, from universal smallpox vaccination to making the police work, Ajay Shah applies four tests. The higher a job scores on each, the harder it is.
The first is the number of transactions. A government might put out 500 research grants a year, he said, while polio vaccination means touching 500 million people. {#polio}

The second is the discretion of frontline workers. “We are all deeply wired to be kind to our friends and family and our kids and kin,” Shah said, so discretion is often used against the organisation’s objectives.
These two came from Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock. Vijay Kelkar and Shah added the other two.
## Stakes and secrecy
A policeman who can put you in jail is in a high-stakes conversation with you. Someone giving a child polio drops has nothing to gain: low stakes.
Then opacity. Body cams, published statistics, the CAG and RTI let journalists, researchers and opposition parties kick up a fuss. Without them, Shah said, “like anything can be done”. {#rti}
~ Amit Varma saw one thread running through all four: the gap between the objectives of the state and the incentives of its employees. {#thread}

quote.text: We have a clear toolkit and you don’t even need paper and pen. You can just memorise this.

sections.label: Worked examples
sections.head: Six calls a year, or 2,000
sections.caption: monetary policy and taxation
body: Asked by Amit Varma to show, not tell, Ajay Shah began with an op-ed whose title says it all: *Monetary policy is easy; Financial regulation is hard*. {101-R05}

A properly structured monetary policy committee makes six decisions a year to hit a 4 per cent inflation target, and each member writes down why. Low transactions, low discretion, low stakes, no secrecy.
Financial regulation is four on four: a thousand firms, about 2,000 touch points a year, judgment calls on bad loans, billions of dollars at stake, and supervision done in secret. {#touchpoints}
## Filling in the table

Varma then imagined a table and called out rows. Elementary schools have high transactions, and teachers with complete discretion over whether to teach, make eye contact or try three times harder. But a teacher’s wage is modest, so stakes are low, and opacity can be fixed. Two out of four.
A vaccination campaign, for HPV or polio, follows a fixed protocol, and the vaccinator has nothing to gain: easy. {#hpv}
The judiciary has ultimate discretion and ultimate stakes, and judges on a bench deliberate behind closed doors: three and a half out of four. {#judiciary}
~ Taxation, which Varma called Shah’s favourite subject, was the worst: thousands of crores at stake for big accounts, and complete opacity. Four on four. {101-C04}

quote.text: High number of transactions, high discretion in the hands of the tax officer, high stakes, sky high stakes

sections.label: The hacker’s turn
sections.head: Hard problems, hacked
sections.caption: redesigning hard into easy
body: Amit Varma, sure that Ajay Shah is a hacker at heart, asked whether the table itself could be hacked.
It could, Shah said. Stare at a bad row and ask whether the policy can be redesigned to turn a hard problem into an easy one.

Modern monetary policy is the proof. It was once messy and opaque, run by a powerful governor who could do whatever they wanted. An inflation target, a committee dominated by private economists and complete transparency hacked its components. {101-C05}
## The ticket window

Information technology can do the same, Shah argued in a 2005 paper on IT in governance. {#itpaper} High transactions are mostly about pieces of paper: moving them between offices, guarding them against counterfeits. Computerise them, and the problem can go away.
Discretion can be tamed too. When train bookings lived in a paper register, the clerk at the ticket window could say there was no seat. {101-S03} In an open database, seat 2A is either taken or not.
~ That, Shah said, is the real value of an IT system: it removes discretion from the frontline civil servant and converts a component from hard to easy.

quote.text: So we changed our whole paradigm of how to think about this in order to make it easy.

sections.label: The hardest basics
sections.head: Three basics, a century’s work
sections.caption: Adam Smith’s three essentials
body: Amit Varma brought in Francis Fukuyama’s distinction between a state’s scope, how many things it does, and its strength, how well it does them. India’s state is high on scope and low on strength. Is that because the few things it must do well are hard? {101-C09}

Ajay Shah answered with what he called one of the greatest quotes in economics. Adam Smith wrote that little else is needed to carry a state from the lowest barbarism to the highest opulence but “peace, easy taxes, and a tolerable administration of justice”. {101-J10}
## No easy minimal state

Run those through the four tests, Shah said, and every one is very hard. Peace means the military, the police, criminal justice and courts. Taxation and the judiciary already sat at the top of the table.

State capability has a budget constraint, he argued: money, the headcount of civil servants and, above all, the attention of leaders, researchers and reformers. Getting the core right could take 50 to 100 years, so every other calendar entry should get a no. {#century}
~ Varma added that hard is not the same as unimportant. Smith’s three are necessary and practically sufficient, so they must be done however hard they are. {101-C08}

quote.text: both you and I agree that what the Indian State should do is it should do a few things well, not many things badly

side.boxText: Ajay Shah loves *Solutions When the Solution is the Problem* because the question it asked, whether an intervention is easy or hard to implement, was itself a breakthrough. Lant Pritchett and Michael Woolcock wrote it in 2004, proposing the first two tests. {#origin}

contQuote.text: the metrics that we laid out are not metrics for importance, they’re metrics for how hard something is. And just because something is very hard doesn’t mean that it should not be done.

p3.title: Parables of the state
p3.deck: A drunk, a ticket clerk, Nehru in 1947 and an imagined landing

stories.start: And I'm reminded of the metaphor of uh the drunk man who one night
stories.end: yeah, drunk man, lamp post, where did you drop the keys?
stories.caption: the drunk under the lamppost
stories.kicker: Amit Varma’s parable, and his charge against RCTs
stories.head: The key is in the dark
body: One night, a drunk man is searching under a lamppost. A policeman comes up, and Amit Varma was particular about him: “a good policeman in a country with rule of law”. {101-J08}
“My friend, what are you looking for? Can I help you?” the policeman asks. The drunk man is looking for his key, so the policeman, “with great humility and a sense of service”, helps him look.
They search for some time and find nothing. At last the policeman asks where the key was dropped. “Over there in the bushes where it’s very dark,” says the drunk man.
Then why look here? “Because this is where the light is.”
Varma’s worry is that many of us go after easy problems that are inconsequential and do not move the needle, rather than solving the hard ones.

He used the same parable to open his *The Seen and the Unseen* episode with Lant Pritchett, aimed at RCTs in development economics. “RCTs are solving inconsequential, easy problems simply because they’re attributable and measurable,” he said, “and it’s a great fraud on the field of economics.” {101-S05}
The tough problems are difficult and fuzzy, Varma said, “and that’s what a real man tries to solve and Lant Pritchett is a real man”.

~ Later Varma found that the scholar Yuen Yuen Ang had used the same metaphor, almost simultaneously, in her paper *Adaptive Political Economy*. He wrote to her, and says she will be on his show once she finishes a very important book. {101-J15}
stories.why: Measurable, attributable problems tempt us because they let us feel productive, while the problems that matter stay fuzzy and in the dark. It is worth asking whether you work on something because it matters or because it is well lit.

stories.start: In the olden days, the booking status of a given seat
stories.end: frontline civil servant and thereby convert a component from hard to easy
stories.caption: the railway ticket clerk
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on the railway register and the lying clerk
stories.head: Seat 2A, taken or not?
body: In the olden days, Ajay Shah said, the booking status of every seat on every train was kept on paper, in a register inside the railway office. {101-S03}
So the clerk at the ticket window had complete discretion. “He could lie to you,” Shah said. “He could say there’s no ticket here.”

Then the bookings went into a database open to the whole world, ideally through an API, and the discretion was gone. “It’s black and white,” Shah said. “Seat number two A, is it taken? Is it not taken?”
~ The government need not even run IRCTC, he added. It only has to open up an API, and ClearTrip and MakeMyTrip will do the rest. {#api}
stories.why: The real value of a good IT system, Shah said, is that it strips discretion from the frontline civil servant, and so turns a hard component into an easy one.

stories.start: It's a big ask that if somebody says to Javarlal Nehru in 1947
stories.end: it is very hard to do these basics. So don't do mission creep
stories.caption: what Nehru should have heard
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah imagines a different conversation in 1947
stories.head: Hands full, Mr Nehru
body: Imagine, Ajay Shah said, that in 1947 somebody told Jawaharlal Nehru to work on peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice, Adam Smith’s three essentials. {101-S04}
In Shah’s telling, Nehru brushes it off: yes, yes, that is all good, but we also need land reform.

The right answer, Shah argued, would have been alarm: “Wow, peace very hard. Easy taxes, very hard. Tolerable administration of justice, very hard. We have our hands full, we are swamped. Don’t give me anything more to do.”
~ Every extra project, he said, drains money, civil servants and the attention of leaders from a core that could take 50 to 100 years to get right. {#century}

quote.text: Our conclusion should be that it is very hard to do these basics. So don’t do mission creep.

stories.start: So let's start at a military analogy. Suppose we're in a discussion where
stories.end: Amazingly enough, the answer is yes, we do have this kind of toolkit
stories.caption: landings in Burma and China
stories.head: Burma yes, China no
body: Picture a hypothetical Indian expeditionary force, Ajay Shah said, weighing landings in Burma against landings in China. {101-S01}

In a flash, we know the answer. Both are very hard. But push comes to shove, a sufficiently complex Indian naval operation could land troops in Burma, while landings in China are practically impossible.
“Watch what we just did,” Shah said. “We discussed a problem statement and we arrived at a judgment that is this easy or is this hard.”

~ Could the same quick call be made about the clamour of demands on the state: to manipulate the exchange rate, stabilise inflation, build an atom bomb or run polio vaccination? “Amazingly enough,” Shah said, “the answer is yes.” {#yes}
stories.why: We already judge feasibility at a glance in some fields. The four tests make that move routine for policy, so that proposals are weighed on whether they can work, not just on whether they are desirable.

quiz.q: Which four tests does Ajay Shah apply to judge how hard a state intervention is?
quiz.a: Transactions, frontline discretion, stakes and opacity: the higher each scores, the harder the job.

quiz.q: How many decisions a year must a modern monetary policy committee get right?
quiz.a: Six, which is why Shah calls monetary policy a trivial, easy problem.

quiz.q: Which job did Shah score “four on four”, with stakes of thousands of crores?
quiz.a: Taxation: high transactions, high discretion, sky-high stakes and complete opacity.

quiz.q: What were Adam Smith’s three requirements for carrying a state from barbarism to opulence?
quiz.a: Peace, easy taxes and a tolerable administration of justice, each very hard.

quiz.q: Why could the old railway ticket clerk tell you there were no seats?
quiz.a: Bookings sat in a paper register, giving him complete discretion to lie.

quiz.q: In Amit Varma’s parable, why does the drunk search under the lamppost?
quiz.a: Because that is where the light is, though the key fell elsewhere.
